title: Business & Work Shorts
chapters: Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes

units.t: Business & Work Shorts.
In this episode: The 80/20 rule: the vital few and Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes.
Part one. The 80/20 rule: the vital few.
A few customers bring most of the sales, a few problems cause most of the headaches.
The 80/20 rule is one of the most useful ideas in business, and one of the most misunderstood.
From Pareto to Juran.
Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian engineer turned economist, studied data on wealth and income in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
He noticed that a small fraction of people owned a very large share of the land.
In Italy, roughly 80 per cent of the land was held by about 20 per cent of the population, and he found similar patterns elsewhere.
A tale about pea pods in his garden is hard to verify.
Pareto never proposed a universal rule.
That came decades later from Joseph Juran, a quality pioneer who found a few causes produced most manufacturing defects.
He called them the vital few, as opposed to the trivial many, later the useful many, and named the idea after Pareto.
He later acknowledged he had stretched Pareto's work.
What the rule says.
At heart the Pareto principle is a simple observation: inputs and outputs are often unequal.
A minority of causes frequently produces most of the results.
In a typical business, a small group of customers may account for most of the revenue, a few products for most of the profit, or a handful of recurring faults for most of the complaints.
The numbers 80 and 20 are a memorable shorthand, not a law of nature.
The real split might be 70/30, 90/10 or 95/5.
The two numbers also do not have to add up to 100, because they measure different things: one is the share of causes, the other the share of effects.
Using it at work.
The practical power of the Pareto principle is in deciding where to look first.
Quality engineers use a Pareto chart, a bar chart that sorts problems from most to least frequent, to show which few causes deserve attention.
A cafe owner might find that a handful of menu items make most of the money, and simplify the rest.
A support team might find that most calls are about a few common issues, and fix those with clearer instructions.
In personal work, it suggests asking which tasks truly move a project forward, and doing those before polishing the details.
The question is not how to do everything, but which few things matter most.
Where people go wrong.
Because it is catchy, the principle is often misused.
Some people treat 80/20 as an exact law and assume the numbers without measuring anything.
Others conclude the remaining 80 per cent of customers, tasks or products can simply be dropped.
That can be a serious mistake.
Small customers may become large ones, cheap products may draw people into a store, and routine tasks such as paperwork, safety checks and maintenance can have serious consequences if neglected.
Juran's later phrase, the useful many, was a deliberate correction.
The principle works best as a prompt to gather data and look for imbalances, not as an excuse to ignore everything outside the top fifth.
Why the world is lopsided.
Why do so many things follow this lopsided pattern?
One reason is that success compounds.
A popular product gets better shelf space, more reviews and more word of mouth, which makes it more popular still.
A big customer may grow faster because it already has scale.
In networks such as cities, websites and social media, a few hubs attract a large share of the connections.
Mathematicians describe such distributions as heavy-tailed or power laws, and they appear in fields from earthquakes to book sales.
This helps explain why averages can mislead.
When a few cases dominate the total, the typical case may look very different from the average one.
The key idea: Pareto noticed unequal wealth in Italy, and Joseph Juran later turned the idea into a general management rule.
Part two. Psychological safety: why the best teams admit mistakes.
A researcher expected the best hospital teams to make the fewest errors.
Her data said the opposite, and that surprise changed how we think about teamwork.
A puzzling result.
In the 1990s researcher Amy Edmondson studied medication errors in hospital teams.
She expected teams with better leadership and stronger relationships to make fewer mistakes.
The data seemed to show the reverse: the better teams reported more errors.
Then she realised what might be happening.
The best teams were probably not making more mistakes.
They were more willing to talk about them, while in teams where people feared blame, errors were hidden.

That insight led to psychological safety, which Edmondson, later a Harvard Business School professor, defines as a shared belief in a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as asking a question, admitting a mistake or raising a concern.
Google's Project Aristotle.
In 2012 Google launched Project Aristotle to find out what made some of its teams more effective than others.
Researchers studied around 180 teams, expecting the right mix of skills, personalities or backgrounds to explain success.
Those factors mattered far less than expected.
What mattered most was how team members interacted.
When Google published its findings in 2015, it listed five key dynamics: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact.
Psychological safety was described as by far the most important, the foundation the others depended on.
The findings drew wide attention and brought Edmondson's work to a far larger audience.
Not about being nice.
A common misunderstanding is that psychological safety means lowering expectations or avoiding criticism.
Edmondson is clear that it does not.
It also does not mean everyone agrees.
It describes the climate of a group, not one person's confidence: the same person might speak freely in one team and stay silent in another.
It means honest disagreement and bad news surface early, while there is still time to act.
She describes a grid.
Low safety and low standards produce apathy.
High safety with low standards is comfortable but unstretching.
High standards with low safety produces anxiety, and people hide problems.
The goal is high standards with high safety, her learning zone.
Candour and kindness are not opposites.
Why silence is dangerous.
The cost of silence can be enormous.
Investigations into accidents in aviation, healthcare and engineering have often found that someone saw a warning sign but hesitated to raise it with a more senior person.
From around the 1980s aviation responded with crew resource management training, which teaches junior crew to voice concerns clearly and captains to invite them.
In business the costs are usually quieter but still real: a flawed product nobody challenged, a project everyone privately doubted, a safety shortcut nobody reported.
Fear does not stop problems happening.
It mostly stops leaders hearing about them until they are much bigger and more expensive to fix.
Building it in your team.
Psychological safety can be built, and leaders have the biggest influence.
Edmondson suggests three broad practices.
First, frame the work as a learning problem rather than simple execution, being honest that there is uncertainty and that everyone's input is needed.
Second, acknowledge your own fallibility, with something as simple as saying you might be missing something.
Third, model curiosity by asking genuine questions.
Just as important is how you react when someone speaks up.
Thanking a person for raising a problem, even unwelcome news, encourages others to do the same.
Reacting with anger teaches the whole team to stay quiet.
Trust is built slowly and can be damaged very quickly.
The key idea: Amy Edmondson found that better hospital teams reported more errors, because they felt safe to speak up.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Joseph Juran add to Pareto's observation?
Answer. He generalised it into a rule that a few causes drive most problems.
Question two. Why did the better hospital teams report more errors?
Answer. They were more willing to talk about mistakes.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
